question: The aerodynamic part of the flight warning system alerts the crew to deviations in:

options.text: Engine temperature and vibration
Heading, track and drift
Cabin altitude, fuel quantity and engine oil pressure
Altitude, airspeed and angle of attack

explanation: It provides the altitude alerting system, the overspeed warning and the stall warning, covering altitude, airspeed and angle of attack.

question: The function of the altitude alerting system is to warn the pilots that the aircraft is:

options.text: Approaching or leaving the MCP altitude
Close to terrain ahead of the aircraft
Above its certified maximum altitude
Below the minimum safe altitude for the area being flown

explanation: It warns within height bands above and below the MCP selected altitude, both on approach to that altitude and on deviating from it. Terrain warnings come from the GPWS.

question: Typical altitude alerting bands are:

options.text: 100–300 ft in all aircraft
1000–2000 ft in all aircraft
300–900 ft in one system, 250–750 ft in another
50–500 ft in one system, 500–1000 ft in another

explanation: Typical bands are 300 to 900 ft for one manufacturer's aircraft and 250 to 750 ft for another's.

question: In a 300–900 ft system, approaching the selected altitude, what happens at 900 ft to go?

options.text: The altitude box turns amber, with a continuous caution beeper
A white box and a short alert
The autopilot starts to level off
The master caution lights come on

explanation: At 900 ft before the selected altitude a white box appears around the current altitude on the PFD with a momentary alert. It disappears at 300 ft to go.

question: When the aircraft deviates 300 ft from the selected altitude, the system gives:

options.text: Master caution, beeper and an amber box
A red master warning and a siren
A synthetic voice calling "altitude, altitude" repeatedly
Only a white box, with no sound

explanation: At 300 ft deviation the master caution lights come on, a continuous beeper sounds, ALTITUDE ALERT appears and the altitude box turns amber: a level B caution.

question: The deviation alert stops when the aircraft:

options.text: Returns to within 100 ft of the selected altitude again
Has been away from the altitude for 30 seconds
Returns within 300 ft, or passes 900 ft
Climbs or descends at more than 1000 fpm

explanation: It ceases on return to within 300 ft of the selected altitude, or when the deviation exceeds 900 ft. The aural alert and master caution can be cancelled by pressing the light.

question: A deviation of more than 300 ft from the selected altitude generates:

options.text: No alert, only a white box
A level B alert
A level C alert
A level A alert

explanation: It is a caution (level B): an EICAS message, an alert tone, and the amber master caution and ALT ALERT lights.

question: Altitude alerting is inhibited:

options.text: Whenever the autopilot is engaged in any mode
Below the transition altitude
Above FL290
After G/S capture, or landing flap and gear

explanation: Altitude alerting is inhibited in flight when the glide slope is captured, or when landing flaps are selected with the gear down.

question: For commercial air transport, an altitude alerting system is required in:

options.text: Turbojets only
All aircraft over 2000 kg
Only aircraft certified to fly above FL410
Turbojets, and larger turboprops

explanation: The operating rules require one in turbojet aircraft and in turboprops of more than 5700 kg or more than 9 passenger seats.

question: As a minimum, the required altitude alerting system must alert the crew:

options.text: On approach, and aurally on deviation
Only when deviating, by a light
Only when approaching it, by a synthetic voice message
At every 1000 ft of climb or descent

explanation: It must alert on approaching the preselected altitude and, by at least an aural signal, on deviating above or below it.

question: The overspeed warning alerts the crew when the airspeed exceeds:

options.text: The flap limiting speed only
VNE, taken from the airspeed indicator's red line
VMO or MMO, calculated by the ADC
The maximum tyre speed

explanation: The overspeed warning system alerts the crew if the airspeed exceeds VMO/MMO as calculated by the air data computer.

question: In an aircraft with electronic instruments, an overspeed produces:

options.text: A stick shaker and a cricket sound
A siren, red WARNING lights and OVERSPEED
A white message on the lower display, with no aural alert
An amber master caution and a chime

explanation: The system sounds the siren or horn, lights the red master WARNING lights and shows OVERSPEED in red on the upper EICAS display.

question: The overspeed warning can be silenced by:

options.text: Selecting the test switch
Nothing but reducing speed below the limit
Pressing the master WARNING light switch once
Pressing the master caution light

explanation: The warning continues while the overspeed exists and cannot be cancelled by pressing the master WARNING light.

question: If the overspeed warning system fails:

options.text: A back-up horn sounds at VD
The stall warning system gives the overspeed alert instead
The autopilot limits the speed instead
There is no warning when VMO or MMO is exceeded

explanation: Its input comes from the ADCs via the warning system; if it fails, exceeding VMO/MMO produces no warning. It can be tested before flight.

question: On a conventional airspeed indicator, the maximum allowable speed is shown by:

options.text: A red radial line fixed to the dial
A white triangle
A barber's pole
A yellow arc

explanation: A moving barber's pole shows the maximum allowable speed; on an EFIS it appears on the speed tape.

question: Climbing at constant IAS, the barber's pole:

options.text: Moves to a lower IAS once MMO becomes limiting
Stays at VMO at all altitudes
Moves to a higher indicated airspeed as altitude increases
Disappears above the tropopause

explanation: The pole shows VMO until MMO is limiting; then it moves anticlockwise, because MMO expressed as an IAS decreases as altitude increases.

question: The stall warning system warns when the aircraft approaches:

options.text: The stalling angle of attack
The critical Mach number
A fixed minimum indicated airspeed for the type
The maximum operating altitude

explanation: Stall warning is based on approaching the stalling angle of attack for the current speed and configuration.

question: In the simplest light aircraft stall warning, the sensor is:

options.text: A gyro in the instrument panel
A hinged vane in the wing leading edge
A strain gauge mounted on the main wing spar
A pitot tube under the wing

explanation: A hinged vane protrudes from the leading edge. As angle of attack increases the airflow deflects it until it closes a switch for the cockpit warning.

question: In larger aircraft, the stall warning and prevention systems may include:

options.text: An aileron pusher only
A rudder pedal shaker and a spoiler lock
A thrust lever vibrator
A stick shaker and a stick pusher

explanation: Larger aircraft use more active systems: a stick shaker, and a stick pusher or nudger.

question: The margin between the stall and the stall warning must be at least:

options.text: 2 kt or 2% of the CAS, whichever is greater
5 kt or 5% of the CAS, whichever is less
5 kt or 5% of the CAS, whichever is greater
10 kt or 10% of the CAS, whichever is greater

explanation: The stall warning must start at least 5 kt or 5% CAS above the stall, whichever is greater.

question: In fly-by-wire aircraft, the stall warning consists of:

options.text: A stick shaker only
An amber light and a chime
A cricket, a "STALL" voice and a red light
A siren, a horn and a flashing amber light

explanation: Most aircraft use stick shakers that vibrate the column and rattle. Fly-by-wire systems use a cricket sound, a synthetic "STALL" message and the red master WARNING light.

question: The stall warning must continue until:

options.text: The airspeed rises by 5 kt
The pilot cancels it
The aircraft has descended by 100 ft or more
AoA falls to about the onset value

explanation: The warning must continue until the angle of attack is reduced to approximately the value at which it began.

question: Which inputs does the stall warning module use? (1) Angle of attack; (2) Flap and slat positions; (3) Landing gear weight-on-wheels; (4) Airspeed

options.text: 1 and 2 only
1 and 4 only
1, 2 and 4 only

explanation: The module uses angle of attack, flap and slat positions, air/ground (weight-on) position and airspeed from the ADC.

question: Why is the angle of attack signal modified when flaps or slats are extended?

options.text: They change the stalling angle and the pitch attitude
The stick shaker is too strong with the flaps extended
The vanes are retracted with the flaps
The airspeed sensors are disconnected

explanation: Flap and slat extension changes the aircraft's stalling angle and attitude, so the AoA signal is corrected for their positions, sensed by relays.

question: The stall warning system becomes active during take-off when:

options.text: The gear is retracted
The aircraft passes 400 ft above the runway
The aircraft passes V1
The nosewheel lifts off

explanation: At nosewheel lift-off, microswitches make the stall warning system active.

question: The outputs of the stall warning system may go to:

options.text: The elevator trim and the flaps
The shaker, voice and master WARNING
The autothrottle and the ground spoilers only
The cabin pressure controller

explanation: Outputs may drive a stick shaker motor, an angle of attack indicator, aural and synthetic voice warnings, and the red master WARNING light.
